name: Tetsǫ́t’ıné
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 5 other works consulted do not discuss stress; 2 further works by the same author (or citing it for stress) agree.

catalog_quote: Tetsǫ́t’ıné is a quantity-sensitive, left-to-right iambic system in which high tone attracts stress. If we put aside the role of tone, the interaction between quantity and iambic feet in Tetsǫ́t’ıné is typologically normal for an iambic system (cf. Hayes 1995). Thus, every heavy syllable constitutes the head of a foot. Light syllables can form a foot together with a heavy syllable to their immediate right, or else two light syllables can also form a foot. This is illustrated in the examples in (13). Here, H and L refer to heavy and light syllables, respectively, rather than tones. The coda consonant ɬ does not add coda weight in (13c) and (13d). Note also that we assume that word-final light syllables are extrametrical, as in (13e). [...] The stress pattern in (13) holds true for all words with level tone patterns (i.e. all-low tones or all-high tones). Where words contain a mix of low and high tones, high tone attracts stress, sometimes to a different position than we would expect solely based on the weight patterns in (13). For example, the word (ˈʃé.ne)(ˈthĩː) ‘you eat’ has trochaic stress, due to the initial high tone, despite having the same weight pattern as in (13c). [p. 11] [...] We propose that Tetsǫ́t’ıné stress is iambic by default. Because high tone attracts stress, in accordance with the TSP (DeLacy 2002, 2007), however, a high–low tone pattern will result in a trochee in two-syllable words. [p. 17]
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Chipewyan (chip1261) is not in the catalog. this search of works with stress in the title's only target item, Leer 1976 'Spirantization and the Development of Suprasegmentals in Proto-Athabaskan' (Glottolog 167470 = ANLA CA965L1976b), was located as an open scan on the ANLA server (the ANLA record page loads viahttps://uafanlc.alaska.edu/drupal/api/recordand the file list via search.php?res=; the host has an incomplete certificate chain, downloaded with -k), downloaded (86 scanned pages, no text) and scanned at 200 dpi one tesseract at a time. It is a comparative tonogenesis manuscript (PA constriction/glottalization -> tone in daughter stems); Chipewyan appears only as a tone-reflex language ('in Chipewyan the reflex is high tone with the loss of the final glottal stop', scan p. 18) and the words 'stress'/'accent' do not occur anywhere in the scanned. Relevance: prosody-but-not-word-stress; priority none. From material already held by the project, the best first-hand word-stress statement is Jaker & Howson 2022 (Phonology 39, CC-BY) p. 11: Tetsǫ́t’ıné (a dialect of Dëne Sųłıné) has quantity-sensitive, left-to-right, iterative iambic stress with high tone attracting stress and rightmost stress primary (p. 18); Goddard 1912 pp. 82-83 gives an older, self-described incomplete Cold Lake statement (stress on the semantically important/stem syllable). with updated.

Quote 1 is verbatim on p. 11 (section 3.4 'Distributional evidence for stress', second paragraph: 'Tetsǫ́t’ıné is a quantity-sensitive, left-to-right iambic system in which high tone attracts stress. Light syllables can form a foot together with a heavy syllable to their immediate right, or else two light syllables can also form a foot.' and 'Note also that we assume that word-final light syllables are extrametrical, as in (13e).'); the compiler '[..]' and '[p. 11]' are its own elisions/markers, the wording itself ma…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Left-to-right, quantity-sensitive iambic feet: every heavy (long-vowel or word-final closed) syllable is a foot head; a light syllable groups with a following heavy or light syllable to form a (L ˈH)/(L ˈL) iamb; feet are iterative so words carry more than one stress, and the rightmost stress is (impressionistically) primary. High tone attracts stress, so H–L sequences surface as trochees and a low-toned syllable after a high-toned one is unstressed; final light syllables are extrametrical. Duration is the main acoustic cue, intensity secondary, F0 not a cue (tone is contrastive).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Iterative footing gives more than one stress per prosodic word (e.g. (ˈheː)(ˈtãː) 'they drink', (ja.ˈneɬ)(ˈthiː) 'you speak'); 'Jaker's subjective impression is that where there is more than one stress in a prosodic word, the rightmost stress is the primary stress' (p. 18); the acoustic study found no significant duration or intensity difference between primary and secondary stress (fn. 4, p. 18).
new_statements.exceptions: High tone attracts stress: a high–low tone pattern yields a trochee in disyllables (e.g. (ˈhí.tãː) 'we drink'); a low-toned syllable following a high-toned one is unstressed (final syllable unstressed in L-H-L and H-H-L words, e.g. (he.ˈné)kheː); word-final light syllables are extrametrical ((ˈthaː)ɣe 'three'); coda consonants in prefixes are generally non-moraic except in 1PL hít and 2PL uh, while word-final codas are moraic. Older Cold Lake description (Goddard 1912: 82) instead places accent on the semantically most important syllable (the stem in verbs) with some words always final-stressed and many words with two accents, and calls itself 'quite incomplete'.
new_statements.domain_note: Prosodic word; verbs only in the acoustic study (all stems obligatorily heavy and word-final); citation-form verb paradigms elicited from four Tetsǫ́t’ıné speakers in Yellowknife and Łutselk’e. Ordinary (non-neutralising) case: stress position adjusts to fixed tone and vowel length; a minority of cases show tone shift, vowel-length transfer and consonant deletion driven by iambic footing (§3.4).
new_statements.identity_note: The deciding statement describes Tetsǫ́t’ıné, the Yellowknives Dene dialect of Dëne Sųłıné spoken at Dettah/N'dilo and Łutselk'e, NWT (ISO chp; Jaker & Howson 2022 p. 4: 'a dialect of Dëne Sųłıné'). Glottolog 5.1 lists three chip1261 dialects — Eastern Chipewyan east2857, Western Chipewyan west2954, Old Yellowknife Chipewyan oldy1234 — the last being the historical Yellowknife variety; the modern Tetsǫ́t’ıné has no separate glottocode, so the entry should be filed under chip1261 with the dialect flagged. The older Cold Lake (Alberta) dialect statement of Goddard 1912: 82 (semantic/stem-based accent, some final-stress words, two accents per word) is impressionistic and self-described as incomplete; Cook 2004 (Cold Lake-based grammar) was not accessible and may give a different language-level statement.

new_statements.quote: Data from two northern Dene languages, Tetst’ıné (ISO: CHP) and Wıìlıìdeh (ISO: DGR) complicate this simple generalization. These two languages have nearly identical tonal phonologies, but with opposite tones. Early in the derivation, iambic stress attracts High tone in Tetst’ıné, but Low tone in Wıìlıìdeh. However, later in the derivation, High tone attracts stress in both languages.

tone_statements.citation: Tufts, Kody. 2023. Dene Sųłiné Non-Segmental Morphology: Implications for Morphological Theory. MA thesis (Linguistics), University of Calgary. doi:10.11575/PRISM/41508; hdl:1880/116665.
tone_statements.quote: Notable phonological features include contrastive series of plain, aspirated, and ejective stops and affricates (e.g. Dene Sųłiné [t], [tʰ], and [t’]), and the use of contrastive tone. Many languages of the family, including Dene Sųłiné, contrast a single marked tone with an unmarked tone (Kingston 2005) ... Dene Sųłiné’s system of lexical tone is demonstrated by minimal pairs such as ya ‘sky’ vs. yá ‘lice’ and tha ‘marten’ vs. thá ‘long time’ (Cook 2004: 6), with high tone marked orthographically by the acute diacritic. The marked high tone is also employed in nominal and verbal inflection, as, for example, in the pair of nouns ke ‘shoe’ and seké ‘my shoe’ wherein high tone is one indicator of possession (Cook 2004: 117) ...
tone_statements.locator: §1.3 'Linguistic characteristics', pp. 3–4; grammatical H described §1.6 pp. 12–16 and §2.1.1 pp. 17–18 (ex. 14 danedá 'sits down' vs danéda 'sat down')
tone_statements.summary: Two tones: marked High (acute accent) vs unmarked Low, lexically contrastive on vowels (syllable nuclei); High tone additionally serves as an inflectional exponent — possession marking on nouns and a perfective 'H' realised on the penultimate syllable of certain third-person perfective verb forms (contrast danedá IPFV vs danéda PFV), alongside a nasal exponent N; no statement on stress, downstep…

tone_statements.citation: Jaker, Alessandro. 2022. Tetsǫ́t’ıné prefix vowel length: Evidence for systematic underspecification. Natural Language & Linguistic Theory 41(2): 611–653. doi:10.1007/s11049-022-09550-5
tone_statements.quote: Despite being bimoraic, full (long) vowels in stems may contrast only two tones, High or Low. However, long vowels in prefixes contrast four tones: High, Low, Rising, and Falling (TVG Sect. 2). This distribution is expected if the tone bearing unit in Dene languages is neither the syllable nor the mora but rather the Laryngeal node located beneath each segment (Rice 2000b). My transcription of contour tones in prefixes reflects the representation in (13). Thus, High, Low, Rising, and Falling tones in prefixes are transcribed as <áá>, <aa>, <aá>, and <áa>, respectively.
tone_statements.locator: Sect. 2 'Background on Tetsǫ́t’ıné', paragraph following (12) 'Representation of surface vowel length in prefixes' (unpaginated)
tone_statements.summary: H vs L: stem long vowels bear only H or L, long prefix vowels H, L, Rising, Falling, contours written as H/L sequences over two vowel slots (TBU = laryngeal node). Floating H on s/n conjugation markers; pre-/post-accenting prefixes; H deletes in weak iambic position. 30+ tone-marked forms.

tone_statements.quote: The basic C-H pattern with high tone from constriction or glottalization, and low tone in its absence, has been called “high-marked” by Leer ... The acute or high-marked area includes Chipewyan, Beaver, Slave, Kaska, Northern Tutchone, Hare-Bearlake-Mountain, and also Chilcotin.
tone_statements.locator: ms p. 11, sec. 3 'Geography; Map' (C-H = Chipewyan-Hare pattern, defined sec. 2, ms p. 10)
tone_statements.summary: Survey: Chipewyan is 'high-marked': high tone on PA constricted (glottalized) stem vowels, low otherwise, the reverse of Navajo (ms pp. 5, 8-9). No tone count stated; sec. 6.1 and p. 59 suggest some stem vowels neutralize to mid. Data from Li 1933b noun tables (40+ forms). Nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Jaker, Alessandro. 2020. On the historical source of a ~ u alternations in Dëne Sųłıné optative paradigms. Glossa: a journal of general linguistics 5(1): 67. 1–33. doi:10.5334/gjgl.1061
sources.quote: I propose that Pre-Dëne Sųłıné was a quantity-sensitive, left-to-right iambic language; as part of this system, the strong grade of the optative was used in the strong position of an iambic foot, while the weak grade of the optative was used in the weak position of an iambic foot. [p. 7] [...] The stress and foot boundaries shown in column (b) are based on my own subjective impression; however, my intent in including these is to illustrate that, in the modern language, the selection of the strong or weak grade of the optative bears no direct relation to the position of surface stress [p. 22] [...] I suggest that, broadly speaking, the allomorphy is conditioned by stress. /wʌ/ is the default or “elsewhere” allomorph, because, being a light syllable, it can fit into the weak position of an iambic foot. However, /wuː/ is chosen where the syllable needs to be stressed or heavy for independent reasons. [p. 28]

sources.citation: Goddard, Pliny Earle (1912). Analysis of Cold Lake Dialect, Chipewyan. Anthropological Papers of the AMNH 10(2): 67-170. [Not in the target list; already held by the project; read here.]
sources.quote: p. 82: 'Something resembling the stress accent of English is heard with considerable regularity in Chipewyan. As has been said in the preceding section it rests on the syllable having the greater importance as to the meaning of the word. ... A few words like e na', Cree (Fig. 73) and dün ni', moose (Fig. 88) are always accented on the final syllable. The latter word may be a verb form with the stem -ni "to make a noise" and have the accent on the stem as is usual in verbs. Many words have two accents ...' p. 83: 'The above statement is quite incomplete for the subject of stress is difficult in any case ...'
sources.note: Early kymographic description of Cold Lake Chipewyan: stress falls on the semantically most important syllable (the stem in verbs; e.g. dlo'ne 'mouse' initial, dün ni' 'moose' final), many words carry two accents; the author calls his statement incomplete. Consistent with a morphologically anchored (stem) stress rather than a fixed edge position.

sources.quote: One of the major purposes of this paper is to formulate a hypothesis of the development of tone in modern Athabaskan from an earlier (pre-Proto-Athabaskan) system of vowel nuclei ... [scan p. 18:] In most cases the tone reflex of syllables with final glottal stop agrees with that of the constricted vowels: in Navajo, Sarcee, and Kutchin the reflex is generally low tone, whereas in Chipewyan the reflex is high tone with the loss of the final glottal stop.
sources.locator: scan p. 18 (typescript section B; no printed page numbers survive scanned); scan pp. 2-4 introduction
sources.note: Nothing. The manuscript is a comparative-historical study of tonogenesis (Proto-Athabaskan constriction/glottalization of stem vowels and stem-final consonants -> high vs low tone in the daughter languages); Chipewyan appears only as one of thirteen reflex languages for tone. The scan (86 pages: handwritten draft + typescript) has no text; after scanned at 200 dpi the words 'stress' and 'accent' occur nowhere in the text. sources.citation: Tufts, Kody. 2023. Dene Sųłiné Non-Segmental Morphology: Implications for Morphological Theory. MA thesis (Linguistics), University of Calgary. doi:10.11575/PRISM/41508; hdl:1880/116665.
sources.quote: Notable phonological features include contrastive series of plain, aspirated, and ejective stops and affricates (e.g. Dene Sųłiné [t], [tʰ], and [t’]), and the use of contrastive tone. Many languages of the family, including Dene Sųłiné, contrast a single marked tone with an unmarked tone (Kingston 2005) ... Dene Sųłiné’s system of lexical tone is demonstrated by minimal pairs such as ya ‘sky’ vs. yá ‘lice’ and tha ‘marten’ vs. thá ‘long time’ (Cook 2004: 6), with high tone marked orthographically by the acute diacritic. The marked high tone is also employed in nominal and verbal inflection, as, for example, in the pair of nouns ke ‘shoe’ and seké ‘my shoe’ wherein high tone is one indicator of possession (Cook 2004: 117) ...
sources.locator: §1.3 'Linguistic characteristics', pp. 3–4; grammatical H described §1.6 pp. 12–16 and §2.1.1 pp. 17–18 (ex. 14 danedá 'sits down' vs danéda 'sat down')
sources.note: Two-way lexical tone contrast, a single marked high tone vs unmarked (low) tone, minimal pairs ya/yá, tha/thá; high tone also grammatical (possession on nouns; perfective H on the penult of certain 3rd-person perfective verb forms); thesis analyses this inflectional H (and nasality N) in PFM vs DM; no word-stress statement.

sources.citation: Jaker, Alessandro. 2022. Tetsǫ́t’ıné prefix vowel length: Evidence for systematic underspecification. Natural Language & Linguistic Theory 41(2): 611–653. doi:10.1007/s11049-022-09550-5
sources.quote: Despite being bimoraic, full (long) vowels in stems may contrast only two tones, High or Low. However, long vowels in prefixes contrast four tones: High, Low, Rising, and Falling (TVG Sect. 2). This distribution is expected if the tone bearing unit in Dene languages is neither the syllable nor the mora but rather the Laryngeal node located beneath each segment (Rice 2000b). My transcription of contour tones in prefixes reflects the representation in (13). Thus, High, Low, Rising, and Falling tones in prefixes are transcribed as <áá>, <aa>, <aá>, and <áa>, respectively.
sources.locator: Sect. 2 'Background on Tetsǫ́t’ıné', paragraph following (12) 'Representation of surface vowel length in prefixes' (unpaginated)
sources.note: H vs L: stem long vowels bear only H or L, long prefix vowels H, L, Rising, Falling, contours written as H/L sequences over two vowel slots (TBU = laryngeal node). Floating H on s/n conjugation markers; pre-/post-accenting prefixes; H deletes in weak iambic position. 30+ tone-marked forms.
sources.venue: Natural Language & Linguistic Theory
